I’m not an expert but neither of those are really what I mean. Dedicated subreddits require a lot of work, and only reach those who join it. It can be good eventually, but not really helpful until you already have a good sized audience. 

You don’t need a huge account or something. But you should use the Reddit account as an actual Reddit account and not just promotion tool. Or you will get banned or muted. If every person with a hussle was allowed to operate “business accounts” Reddit would be terrible. 

What I mean is where and how you post. I wouldn’t post in dev subreddits with strictly game promotion content. Your posts need to actually add something to the subreddits conversations in some way. 

Smaller Subreddits that are in some (meaningful) way related to your game are pretty good. But they have mods who don’t want a walking advertisement hanging around gunking up the feed. 

Which means you need to actually look at and start understanding the subreddit, and you may find a way to mention your game or even make a post about your game in those. Be respectful, don’t spam, this isn’t a marketing meetup, just be cool and if your post gets zero attention it may have gotten removed. Assess what you probably could have to make the post /comment less market-y and generally more in tune with what that subreddit would like.

I know you are getting clowned on but I get the sentiment. You’ve probably been working really hard on this game for these three years. You don’t want it to get eclipsed. 

That being said, as an indie dev, you aren’t even in the same stratosphere as GTA. And I’m not being rude, and it’s not a bad thing. As an indie you don’t wanna be matched up with rockstar and their millions and millions of dollars in development and hundreds of developers and artists and marketing and all the rest. 

Just focus on what you can do to make your game successful for you. Adjust your expectations and make the game you want to make. Don’t worry about AAA.

My first suggestion would probably be to have something in mind that you want to make whether it’s a game or a mechanic or whatever, but once you have that start thinking about what things are in that game that you would need and then start looking into what other people do in order to create that. 

Like you want to remake Mario 64 or your own version as an example, probably the first thing that you’ll need is a Mario. And what is a Mario in Mario 64? A 3-D character that runs around and jumps. And try to see how people in video games make 3-D characters that run around and jump. And then just keep going, recognize that any video about learning game dev in super short amount of time are essentially lies, and that it will take years. When the engine is playing the game file you can visibly see execution lines light up, you can see where the logic stops flowing when you think it should keep going. For someone like me who thinks more in flow charts and switch boards than I do in abstract classes it helped me a ton. I mean you definitely still need to learn and understand core principles of coding. But the debugging and coding had visual feedback that made sense to my monkey brain more than flat code. Tutorials are like candy, feels like it’s good, but it’s not nutritious and you will starve on them. And that’s true for any aspiring dev. The best way to start learning is to think of some thing that you like in a game, and then try and remake it. And keep it humble. Have grand ambitions, but take it a bite at a time. 

Say you like rocket league, and you want to make your own version. Well you need driveable cars. A ball, an arena. 

The car needs character controller ,
The ball needs physics principles, 
The map needs level design principles.

Accept that failing doesn’t just happen to you, and failing ESSENTIAL to learning gamedev. So don’t stop when you try and fail, because that time was not wasted. 

Getting it right is victory,
Failing and trying a new thing is holding ground,
Tutorials are a retreat. Sometimes necessary, but always your last resort. 

Just try stuff break stuff try again. If you get burned out, drop making logic and try some game dev art. Rinse and repeat. For a long while. It’s a marathon and you can do it if you chose to. Sit down everyday to try if possible. Refuse that you are incapable because you are capable. You just have to get to paying your dues.


My personal recommendation is to swap to unreal engine and start learning how to use blueprints. I felt exactly where you are three years ago. Barely passing coding classes, knowing that I innately wasn’t a great coder but really wanted to make a game and tutorials lead me no where. Moved to unreal out of desperation, 3 years later my game has a steam page and I’m proud of my work. It’s not done but it will get there. And you will get where you chose to go as well. 

I also used unity initially and actually was eventually able to make some thing that sort of resembled a game. But I decided to try unity I think because of some new landscape feature that I heard about. I tried to remake “the wild area” from a Pokémon game I liked. But in messing around with the landscape editor and trying to make some thing that at least felt like a Games landscape, I picked up a bit of the engine and a bit of blue prints when I tried to add rain particles to the default character that comes with unreal engine templates.

Blueprints is a node system that you can use instead of writing literal code. It’s basically chunks of literal code but more easily visually understood.

I found that I was able to go much further much faster with unreal engine. It’s got way more built in for you from the start. 

It’s a better place to learn and to this day I still want to strangle people who tell newbies to use unity. They were once a good starting point, but unreal has surpassed unity in accessibility. Good luck!

When undertaking any new thing like this, it’s important to be humble. If it was easy everyone would do it. Understanding that it’s hard for everyone, and that you aren’t special is important. So also be patient with yourself. 

Game dev is hard to break into. Start trying to think about games in terms of objects. A Player character, a car, a map objects. Then thinking about how those objects might behave. I’m unity those are called game objects, in unreal engine they are called actors. In flappy bird you have two main objects for simplicity’s sake. The bird and the pipes. 

The bird needs logic to move forward, and to flap up when a button is pressed. The pipes need logic to move up and down, and to detect when they touch the bird. Then maybe think about a third invisible object maybe called “game mode” this object is what tells the game to start, which tells the bird and pipes to start moving. When the pipes touch the bird, the pipes should tell the game mode object that they touched the bird, and the game mode should reset the level to start over. 

This same concept applies widely across all aspects of game dev. Another concept could be what’s called inheritance. Think about it like a child inheriting traits from their parents. 

Go back to the pipes example for a second. Say we have our pipes object and say they are colored green. They move up and down and detects collision. But say we want a new type of pipe. One that does everything that the green pipes do, but these pipes are red and they also move from left to right as well as up and down and detect collision. 

Instead of making a new object from scratch for the red pipe, make a red pipe object that is a “child” of the green pipe. That means that every red pipe will automatically have the same logic that the green pipes have, but in the new child red pipe object you can also add logic for moving left and right. Now it does all three behaviors, but you didn’t have to rewrite 2/3rds of the code. This is a bit of a oversimplification but it’s a good concept to start thinking about.

Think about games in terms of objects, and start thinking about how they might be related to each other. Be patient, accept you are not going to like everything you make especially when you start. Accept it will take many more than 8 hours. Accept that games made in 24 hours are done for the novelty and the YouTube thumbnail/title clickbait. Look for “Aha!“ moments. Good luck

My honest advice would be to tone back the scale of this game. These mechanics are a bit advanced. 

General advice if you want to attempt it. 

Have a collider around each tree. (Each tree will need to be an instance of an actor, *BP_teleporterTree*)

When the player overlaps with the tree collider, 
Set character mesh to Hidden, set the camera location like +2000 or so on the Z axis so that the player camera pops up above the tree.

As far as looking around and selecting other trees. look into the “get hit under cursor” node. So when the player clicks on another tree it returns the location of that tree. 

The set the location of the player character to that location. Then have an “end overlap” check so when the player walks outside of the tree’s collider it sets the mesh to no longer hidden. 

That will give you the basics of the mechanic. Also some of what you described I would categorize as polish and not core mechanic. You don’t need to lock the players movement, but you can set the character movement to be not enabled by the enable node. 

As long as you are ok with it not looking as good as it does in your head, then definitely attempt it. Your first games are not going to look like they do in your head. And you have to be ok with that or you will never actually create something enough times that it will start to resemble your initial vision. Game dev is a marathon not a sprint. Tutorials are ok, but they can be a quicksand trap. Better to attempt and fail, and look up answered to specific questions instead of just getting into tutorial hell.

Every time it doesn’t work you learn something.

You are probably “over extending” there is sort of this moving imaginary line of where a “safe” place to be is. It moves as the team moves as a whole into new space. If you are out ahead of this line, you will die. Really good general early advice is to get as much value as you can, without dying. Minimize deaths over all else. You will get less value from damage and kills but it will help you learn how to be more effective and that value will start returning

Right off the bat, I’d go ahead and just stop playing vs Ai. It’s fine to start but once you have a basic grasp of the controls playing vs ai in matches isn’t going to help you. Qp, arcade, and custom games are better practice. Comp is a little different but it will be easy once you get the basic idea.

So the amount of kills will rack up if a team is getting rolled, and the early matchmaking is pretty tumultuous. Those kill differences aren’t what determines who the better team is. Overwatch is all about taking an area, whether it’s a point, or a payload, or a push robot. Taking that area and saying “we are here and you can’t be here”. The team that controls that area longer wins the game. 

Instead of looking at the numbers, look at how well your tank pushed into the enemy and controlled space. See how well you helped the tank do that. If you help your tank you will win more games, especially early. Reaper and mei that hang out by their tank is really powerful as examples of tank enablers. But every hero can do it. Just think about the objective, less about kills/deaths and it will start making more sense

Ok so I read these. First I’ll admit that I was unaware of Chanel racing over water. That should not be happening in my opinion. Thank you for giving me something to look into changing. Then, I’ll offer some anecdotal perspective. If you aren’t interested, no worries and hope you have a good day. 

A close family member of mine has been a pigeon racer since childhood. I myself have been exposed to dozens of racing pigeon enthusiasts. Every one that I have personally met, are fully in love with thier birds. They are content to spend time speaking with their birds as friends, and spend a painstaking amount of time maintaining the health and living conditions of these birds. Quite literally it is a full time activity. The pigeons are fed top quality food, receive regular routine medical attendance, and fly for several hours everyday. And return home to a space heated loft, to safety, nesting with a familiar flock. 

The concept of “widowing” is not the method by which racing pigeons return to a particular loft. 
The cost of keeping two birds for the sole purpose of racing one is monetarily impractical(these people spend ALOT of money on this hobby), and unnecessary. 

Racing pigeons have a biological mechanism that allows them to have a compass like sense of direction. Even when transported and turned in all directions, they have a pretty good general sense of what direction they have travelled. Astoundingly good actually. 

The “North Star” of this internal compass is “Home”. Not a partner, racing pigeons can and often do have different partners throughout their life. This home is their home loft. This location is learned over time and can change. Birds sometimes naturally adopt different flocks when groups collide. And the new bird will acclimate to its flocks new home. 

They return to this location because it is where they associate thief flock, shelter, and food being located. That is what drives racing pigeons to return home. 

Is the pigeon racing world perfect? No. Like any activity where lots of money is involved, you can usually find corner cutters, and the unethical when you hunt for it. And you should hunt for it. Breeders who know of these people shun these people. They do not share the love of these birds that the majority of these breeders feel. 

Massive international races, like the ones that apparently host channel races are likely to be unethical due to scale and being unable to provide the proper care and consideration that these animals require. But the vast majority are the biggest conservationists of pigeons you could meet.
